subtype: Approach: reading signals and accepting a no [Thinking]
passage: Himani had decided the rule before she ever spoke to Santosh: whatever the answer, it stays the answer. On the bus to the kasba school she went over it. A clear no, and I say okay, thanks for telling me. A hesitant "um, maybe not" counts as no as well. No second message. No asking Mansi to talk to Santosh. She said it to herself twice while the paddy fields slid past. That afternoon by the school gate she asked, quietly, whether Santosh would like tea at the corner stall on Sunday. Santosh looked at the ground. "I'm not sure. I don't think so." Something dropped in Himani's chest. "Okay. Thanks for saying," she said, and went to catch the bus. The next morning she waved at Santosh as usual.

qa.q: Where did Himani go over her rule?
qa.a: Himani went over it on the bus to the kasba school.

qa.q: What did Himani feel when Santosh said 'I don't think so'?
qa.a: Something dropped in Himani's chest, so she felt disappointed, yet she stayed composed and kept her promise to herself.

qa.q: What other approach could Himani use to read signals before asking, and why?
qa.a: Himani could first chat in a group at a club or school event to see how comfortable Santosh seems, because that gives more information before a direct question.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel about the way Himani handled the answer?
qa.a: Santosh probably feels relieved and respected, because Himani accepted the answer without pushing or sending others.

grounding: The student decides beforehand to take a hesitant or clear refusal at face value, with no pushing, repeated messages or friends applying pressure, and respects the answer.

passage: Note, 10B, Thursday. In the last period Payal asked three classmates to stay in the room after the bell. As the others gathered their bags, she walked to the front with a bunch of flowers and asked Eshaan, in front of about twenty students, if he would go out with her. Someone started clapping. Eshaan went red, looked at the door, laughed and said, "Uh, maybe, thanks," then left with his bag held to his chest. Payal stood holding the flowers while two boys teased her. What I did: I kept both back for a minute, separately. I told Payal her courage was real and that a quiet question lets a person answer honestly. Eshaan said he needed time. I asked the class to leave it alone and will check in with both on Monday.

qa.q: About how many students watched Payal ask Eshaan?
qa.a: About twenty students watched.

qa.q: How did Eshaan seem to feel during the public question, and how sure can the teacher be?
qa.a: Eshaan seemed embarrassed and cornered, shown by going red, looking at the door and the hurried 'maybe, thanks,' though the teacher cannot be sure of his inner state.

qa.q: What quieter approach could Payal use next time, and why?
qa.a: Payal could ask privately, after a club meeting or by a short message, because without an audience Eshaan can answer honestly and comfortably.

qa.q: What is the moment like for Payal afterwards?
qa.a: Payal is likely to feel exposed and hurt, standing with the flowers while classmates tease, whatever Eshaan eventually says. 🤍

grounding: Inspired by films, the student asks in front of the whole class with flowers, and the audience pressure makes a comfortable answer difficult and embarrasses the other person.

subtype: Approach: never acting due to fear of rejection [Pitfall]
passage: Eshaan, since you ask what your Masi Ira was like at sixteen: scared. There was a boy in the next row, Vikram, who lent me his ruler in class nine, and I decided that was a sign. For months I rehearsed in the bathroom mirror. "Would you like to..." Every version had a hole in it. I wrote the sentence down and tore it up. Some days I got as far as his desk and asked about homework instead. Then one winter afternoon I saw Vikram walking to the library with Nalini, the two of them sharing one umbrella and laughing. I stood there holding my perfect sentence like a bag of stones. Vikram never knew. I can't say the answer would have been yes. But by never asking, I made sure of the no.

qa.q: What did Vikram lend Ira in class nine?
qa.a: Vikram lent Ira a ruler.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when Ira saw Vikram walking with Nalini?
qa.a: Ira felt crushed and full of regret, holding the perfect sentence 'like a bag of stones'.

qa.q: What could the young Ira have done instead of rehearsing for months, and why?
qa.a: Ira could have asked once, quietly and simply, accepting yes or no, because a real answer even a no is better than months of waiting.

qa.q: How might Vikram have seen Ira during those months?
qa.a: Vikram probably saw a classmate who sometimes asked about homework and had no idea of the feelings behind it, so there was never a question to answer.

grounding: The student rehearses endlessly and never speaks, and after months the crush starts talking with someone else, so avoiding a no also removes any chance of a yes.

passage:
Dear Yamini,

You said on the phone that I'd never do it, so here is proof. On Friday, after the debate club meeting, when everyone was packing up, I walked over to Karthik and said quietly, "I really like talking with you. Would you want to grab a chai with me one day?" My hands were cold. Karthik blinked, then smiled and said, "I'd like that. Next Saturday?" I said yes and nearly dropped my folder. That was all: two sentences, nobody watching. If he had said no, I had a line ready: "Okay, no problem," and then I'd have gone home. Anyway, I'm telling you first. Wish me luck for Saturday!

Uma

qa.q: When did Uma ask Karthik about chai?
qa.a: Uma asked on Friday, after the debate club meeting.

qa.q: How did Uma feel while asking, and what shows it?
qa.a: Uma was nervous but resolved; cold hands and nearly dropping the folder show the nerves, while the ready line shows the readiness for either answer.

qa.q: What could Uma do if asking in person felt too hard, and why?
qa.a: Uma could send a short private message with the same two sentences, because it is quiet, simple and easy to answer honestly.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel about the way Uma asked?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt comfortable and pleased, since the question was quiet, private and easy to answer either way.

grounding: The student asks quietly in person after a club meeting, saying they like talking with Karthik and asking whether Karthik would like chai together some time.

subtype: Approach: considering family rules and school norms [Thinking]
passage: The sign-up sheet for the Saturday museum trip closed on Wednesday evening, so Yogesh had one night to decide how to ask Preeti. In the flat he thought it through. His parents liked him home before dark and wanted to know where he was going. The school expected students on trips to stay in groups. A film for two was out. More than that, he did not want Preeti to feel cornered. So: the museum trip, daytime, six or seven classmates, and he would tell Mummy that Preeti was in the group. Next morning at the sign-up table he said, "A few of us are sitting together on the museum trip. Want to join?" Preeti looked at the list and picked up the pen. "Put me next to Anita."

qa.q: When did the sign-up sheet for the museum trip close?
qa.a: The sign-up sheet closed on Wednesday evening.

qa.q: What might Yogesh be worried about while thinking it through?
qa.a: Yogesh is worried about his parents' wishes, the school's group rule, safety, and not making Preeti feel cornered.

qa.q: What alternative setting could Yogesh use if there were no museum trip, and why?
qa.a: Yogesh could invite Preeti to a daytime group project at the library, because a group in daylight keeps things safe and comfortable for both.

qa.q: How might Yogesh's parents see the plan?
qa.a: They would likely feel reassured, since it is a daytime group outing and Yogesh is honest about who will be there.

grounding: The student thinks about family expectations and school rules and chooses a daytime group setting, with safety, honesty with parents and comfort for both people in mind.

subtype: Approach: relying on friends as messengers [Pitfall]
passage: This is what I saw in 10B on Tuesday. At lunch Lokesh pulled his friend Ritu aside and said something, and I heard the words "find out." Ritu then went over to the bench where Sonal sits and asked, loudly enough for the row to hear, "Do you like Lokesh?" Sonal looked at the tiffin box and said, "Why is he asking you?" By fourth period people were saying "Sonal likes Lokesh." I never heard Sonal say that. Sonal packed up her things and left early. Lokesh kept glancing at the door. I can't tell what either of them was thinking. I only saw that Sonal stopped talking to the bench group, and that Lokesh never got an answer from Sonal at all. - Nandini

qa.q: Who did Lokesh ask to find out?
qa.a: Lokesh asked Ritu, and Nandini heard the words 'find out.'

qa.q: How did Sonal seem to feel, and how sure can Nandini be?
qa.a: Sonal seemed uncomfortable and embarrassed at being talked about, though Nandini cannot be sure, since Sonal packed up and left early.

qa.q: What more direct approach could Lokesh use instead, and why?
qa.a: Lokesh could ask Sonal quietly in person or by a short private message, so Sonal is asked directly and not discussed.

qa.q: How might it look to Lokesh that no answer came?
qa.a: Lokesh may feel anxious and regretful, having hoped for a quiet answer but getting gossip and silence.

grounding: The student asks a friend to find out if the crush likes him, and the message becomes gossip so the other person feels talked about rather than asked directly.

subtype: Approach: handling a rejection and recovering [Revision]
passage:
Hi Dev,

Update, since you asked. I asked Sunaina to the tea after the debate on Friday. She said, kindly, that she doesn't feel that way about me. I said "Thanks for telling me straight" and meant it, mostly. It stung all evening. Since then: no messages, no hovering. I went to football on Saturday and Sunday and ate too many samosas with the team. On Monday Sunaina said hi in class and I said hi back like always. It felt normal, which was a relief. It still hurts a bit, but less than Friday. See you at practice.

Harsha

qa.q: How did Harsha respond when Sunaina said no?
qa.a: Harsha said 'Thanks for telling me straight.'

qa.q: How does Harsha feel now compared with Friday?
qa.a: Harsha still hurts a bit but less than Friday, and feels relieved that the hello in class felt normal.

qa.q: What other step could help Harsha keep things comfortable in class, and why?
qa.a: Harsha could keep greeting Sunaina in the usual friendly way and stay busy with friends and sport, because that gives space while disappointment fades.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel about Harsha's reaction?
qa.a: Sunaina likely feels relieved and respected, because the no was accepted and the greeting stayed friendly.

grounding: After a polite no, the student thanks her, gives space, spends time with friends and sport, and keeps a normal friendly greeting so the classroom stays comfortable.

passage:
Dear Imran,

Thank you for not laughing when I told you on Sunday. I had been checking my crush's profile every few minutes: during physics, at dinner, at midnight. Last week's test came back with silly mistakes, and I didn't want to admit that a person I barely talk to was taking over my whole head. So I have logged out of the app on my phone and I look once at night, briefly. I also started the model for the science exhibition. The glue and cardboard fill the space that all the thinking used to. It hasn't gone away, but it is quieter. Could you ask me on Friday how it's going?

Kavitha

qa.q: What had Kavitha been checking every few minutes?
qa.a: Kavitha had been checking a crush's profile every few minutes.

qa.q: What worried Kavitha about the thoughts, and what showed it?
qa.a: Kavitha was worried and a little embarrassed that the thoughts were crowding out study, shown by the silly mistakes on last week's test.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha do if the thoughts stay strong, and why?
qa.a: Kavitha could talk to a parent or the school counsellor as well, because more support helps when a worry keeps taking over.

qa.q: How might Imran feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Imran likely feels trusted and glad to help, especially with a request to ask again on Friday.

grounding: Noticing that thoughts about the crush crowd out study, the student limits checking online, tells a trusted person, and puts the energy into a project, which lowers the intensity.

subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
subtype: Approach: deciding values and limits in advance [Thinking]
passage: Farida, come, sit, I'll tell you about my son Devang's first party. I'm Nandini Aunty to you, but that year I was just a nervous mother. The afternoon before, Devang sat on the edge of his bed with a notebook and wrote a short list: no getting in a car with anyone who has been drinking; nothing to try that I can't name. Then a third line: if it goes wrong, I call home and there are no questions that night. He showed it to me, red in the ears. At the party a boy called Tarun jingled car keys at eleven and said he would drop everyone. Devang didn't argue. He told himself, "That's on my list," and rang me from the balcony. My hands shook on the wheel and I was so proud I said nothing. In the car he said, "The list decided, not me."

qa.q: What did Devang write on his list before the party?
qa.a: Devang wrote: no getting in a car with anyone who has been drinking, and nothing to try that he cannot name.

qa.q: How did Devang seem to feel when Tarun offered the lift?
qa.a: Devang seemed steady and clear rather than pressured, since the choice was already on his list.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the safe decision easy, and what more could Devang have set up?
qa.a: Writing the list beforehand made it easy; Devang could also agree a pick-up signal with an adult so leaving needs no explanation.

qa.q: What was it like for Nandini to get the call?
qa.a: Nandini felt worried and proud, with shaking hands, and stayed quiet in the car so Devang did not feel judged.

grounding: Before a party the student decides what he will not do, such as riding with an unsafe driver or trying substances, so that in-the-moment choices follow a rule already thought through.

subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
subtype: Approach: prepared refusal lines and exit plan [Action]
passage: Before Saturday's party, Farida did two things. First, she agreed a code word with Papa: if she texted "How is the mango tree?", he would call and come to pick her up within fifteen minutes, no questions. Second, she practised one short line in the lift: "No thanks, I'm good." At Anirban's flat, near nine, he held out a small vape. "Just one, everyone's had it." "No thanks, I'm good," said Farida, smiling. Anirban shrugged. "Your loss." Her ears felt hot. She went to the kitchen and texted the mango line. Papa rang eight minutes later. "Beta, I need you home." She told the host she had to go, picked up her bag, and was in the car before anyone could ask why.

qa.q: What was the code word text that Farida planned to send?
qa.a: The text was 'How is the mango tree?'

qa.q: How did Farida feel just after refusing Anirban?
qa.a: Farida felt awkward, shown by her hot ears, but stayed calm and had her plan ready.

qa.q: What could Farida do if Anirban kept pushing, and why?
qa.a: Farida could move to another room and send the code text earlier, because leaving does not need an argument or an explanation.

qa.q: How might Papa see the code word plan?
qa.a: Papa likely feels trusted and reassured, since Farida can leave safely and does not have to explain herself.

grounding: The student prepares a short refusal, 'No thanks, I'm good,' and agrees a code word with a parent for pick-up, so leaving needs no argument or explanation.
